ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Charlotte Brontë — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: First prenatal visit at 7 weeks with nausea and vomiting for a week and early weight loss: dating ultrasound, prenatal tests, and a plan for the nausea

text.paragraph: First prenatal visit at 7 weeks with nausea and vomiting for a week and early weight loss: dating ultrasound, prenatal tests, and a plan for the nausea [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: Nausea most of the day for a week and vomiting three or four times a day; she can no longer face meals and has lost about a kilogram. [S]
She is glad of the pregnancy but anxious about her age and about her own health, having lost her mother and her sisters young. [S]
She asks whether she could carry tuberculosis, since it was in her household. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Charlotte Brontë was born on 21 April 1816 in Thornton, Yorkshire, the third of six children of Maria Branwell and her husband, an Anglican clergyman. [D]
Jane Eyre was first published in 1847 under the pseudonym Currer Bell. [D]
Her mother died on 15 September 1821, in the 39th year of her age, after a long and painful illness. [D]
Her mother's illness may have been cancer; one reference work says uterine cancer. The cause is a later interpretation. [R]

Her two elder sisters, Maria and Elizabeth, fell ill at the Clergy Daughters' School at Cowan Bridge and died at home in 1825, Maria on 6 May aged 11 and Elizabeth on 15 June aged 10; reference works give tuberculosis. [D]
Her brother Branwell died on 24 September 1848, aged 31, of several conditions made worse by heavy drinking; tuberculosis is listed among them. [D]
Her sisters Emily and Anne died of tuberculosis, Emily on 19 December 1848 aged 30 and Anne on 28 May 1849 aged 29. [D]
On 29 June 1854 she married Arthur Bell Nicholls, her father's curate, at Haworth. [D]
In late November 1854, after a long walk on the moors to a waterfall that ended in heavy rain, she began to shiver and had a bad lingering sore throat and cold that made her thin and weak. [D]

Early in 1855, after a visit to Gawthorpe and a long walk over damp ground in thin shoes, she was attacked by "new sensations of perpetual nausea, and ever-recurring faintness"; a doctor who was called assigned a natural cause for her indisposition. [D]

text.paragraph: 10 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, moderate (PUQE-24 score 10), with early weight loss, under evaluation for hyperemesis gravidarum

S — Synthetic presenting concern at the index visit, superseded by the hyperemesis gravidarum diagnosis at the sick visit; her documented "perpetual nausea" is D and the hyperemesis reading of it is R.

value.displayName: Supervision of elderly primigravida, unspecified trimester

list.item: First pregnancy at 38 (elderly primigravida), single live intrauterine pregnancy dated by ultrasound at 7 weeks 1 day: active, confirmed [S]
Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, moderate (PUQE-24 score 10), with early weight loss, under evaluation for hyperemesis gravidarum: active, confirmed [S]

First prenatal visit: dating ultrasound; blood count, blood group and antibody screen, rubella immunity, hepatitis B surface antigen, HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis C tests; urine culture; metabolic panel and urinalysis because of vomiting; influenza vaccine; folic acid 0.4 mg daily in place of the iron-containing prenatal vitamin while nausea lasts. Guideline: USPSTF A and B Recommendations (2026); Guidelines for Vaccinating Pregnant Persons (2026) [S]

Nausea and vomiting, step by step: small frequent dry meals, fluids between meals, ginger if she wishes, and avoiding smells that trigger nausea; doxylamine-pyridoxine from today, raised to four tablets a day if needed; then a second drug (metoclopramide, promethazine, or ondansetron after counseling); PUQE-24 score, weight, pulse, blood pressure, and electrolytes at each visit; same-day review if she cannot keep fluids down for 24 hours or loses more than 5 percent of her pre-pregnancy weight. Guideline: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 189: Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy (2018); The Management of Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum (Green-top Guideline No. 69) (2024) [S]

Maternal-fetal medicine consultation for a first pregnancy at 38 with moderate nausea and vomiting and early weight loss: escalation thresholds, aneuploidy screening and diagnostic options, preeclampsia prevention, tuberculosis risk, and the plan for the rest of the pregnancy. Guideline: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 189: Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy (2018); The Management of Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum (Green-top Guideline No. 69) (2024); Screening for Fetal Chromosomal Abnormalities: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 226 (2020); Aspirin Use to Prevent Preeclampsia and Related Morbidity and Mortality: Preventive Medication (2021) [S]

Aneuploidy screening offered to all, with diagnostic testing available: cell-free DNA from 10 weeks, a nuchal translucency scan at 11 to 14 weeks, or chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis; a detailed anatomy scan at 18 to 22 weeks. Guideline: Screening for Fetal Chromosomal Abnormalities: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 226 (2020) [S]

Tuberculosis screening with an interferon-gamma release assay because of tuberculosis deaths in her household; a shielded chest radiograph and treatment decisions only if it is positive. Guideline: Latent Tuberculosis Infection in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]

Mental health: PHQ-9 at intake and the EPDS in each trimester and after any admission, with support for the strain of severe vomiting and for anxiety rooted in family loss. Guideline: Screening and Diagnosis of Mental Health Conditions During Pregnancy and Postpartum (Clinical Practice Guideline No. 4) (2023); Perinatal Depression: Preventive Interventions (2019) [S]

Preeclampsia prevention: low-dose aspirin 81 mg at bedtime from 12 to 16 weeks until delivery if she has one high-risk or more than one moderate-risk factor (she has two: first pregnancy and age 35 or older); blood pressure at every visit. Guideline: Aspirin Use to Prevent Preeclampsia and Related Morbidity and Mortality: Preventive Medication (2021) [S]

Monitoring while nausea and vomiting last: PUQE-24, weight, pulse, and blood pressure at every visit; electrolytes until stable on oral intake; liver tests if abnormal; mood each trimester; antiemetic side effects (drowsiness, restlessness or abnormal movements, constipation, palpitations). Guideline: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 189: Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy (2018); The Management of Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum (Green-top Guideline No. 69) (2024) [S]
Referral to maternal-fetal medicine, Margaret Oyelaran-Hughes, MD, ordered 1855-01-13 [S]
